title: How to start selling on Amazon Germany in 2026: the complete guide
description: Sell on Amazon.de in 2026: €39 plan, FBA fees from €2.33, VAT/OSS, LUCID, GPSR, the end of the €150 customs exemption and your first 90 days.
tldr: The Professional plan costs €39/month excl. VAT; Individual is €0.99 per item. Choose Professional if you expect 40+ sales a month or want ads [s1].
Germany-only FBA fees (July 2026 card) start at €2.33 for light envelopes; a standard parcel up to 900 g costs €3.44 [s4], plus a 1.5% fuel surcharge since April 2026 [s8].
Peak season fee of €0.21–€0.44 per parcel from 15 Oct 2026 to 14 Jan 2027, and Q4 storage at €52.20/m³/month vs €27.54 the rest of the year [s4][s1].
2026 referral cuts: home products 8% up to €20, pet food/clothing and grocery 5% up to €10, clothing 5% up to €15 [s3].
Stock in German warehouses means a German VAT registration; Pan-EU usually means registrations in six countries [s35]. The EU distance-selling threshold is €10,000 [s28].
The EU €150 duty exemption ended on 1 July 2026: €3 duty per low-value item, plus a €2 handling fee from November 2026 [s24][s26].
Before you ship: LUCID packaging registration, GPSR data and an EU Responsible Person, CE documents, and German-language labels and listings.
Rufus is now part of "Alexa for Shopping" on Amazon.de [s21]: clear German listings that answer buyer questions get recommended.

blocks.p: Amazon.de is the biggest Amazon store in Europe and the main door into the European Union (EU) for most new sellers. Marketplace Pulse estimated Amazon.de at **$50.8 billion of gross merchandise value (GMV, the total value of goods sold)** with **151,435 sellers** in its global marketplace review [s14]. GMV is not the same as Amazon's reported revenue, and Amazon does not publish country GMV, so treat any single number as an estimate.

Two things make Germany attractive. First, a large share of sales already goes through independent sellers: one 2025 market review put about **46% of Amazon's German sales with third-party sellers** and about 17% with Amazon's own retail [s16]. Second, Amazon dominates German marketplaces: one estimate gives it a **63% share** of the marketplace segment [s15]. In plain words: if you sell to German online shoppers, most of them will look on Amazon.

blocks.h3: The wider market: growing again, but slowly

blocks.p: German online retail grew in every quarter of 2025, the first time since 2021, according to the trade association bevh [s18]. Growth is moderate, not explosive: **+3.5% in the first half of 2025** [s17] and **+2.8% in Q3 2025** [s18]. Marketplaces did better than online shops in general, with sales up **5.9% in Q2 2025** [s17]. So the pie is growing a little, and marketplaces take a bigger slice each year.

Chinese platforms (Temu, Shein, AliExpress) pushed hard into Germany, and Amazon answered with **Haul**, a low-price store inside the Amazon app. Haul launched in Germany in June 2025, caps prices at **€20**, and most items cost under €10 [s22]. Delivery can take up to two weeks, and shipping is free from €25 (a €3.50 fee below that) [s23]. Important for you: Haul items are bought and imported by Amazon itself, **not listed by third-party sellers** [s22]. Haul does not take your listings, but it does pull cheap, generic products down in price. If your plan is "cheap unbranded gadget", you now compete with Haul and Temu on price. Don't.

blocks.h3: AI shopping: Rufus, now "Alexa for Shopping"

blocks.p: Rufus, Amazon's AI shopping assistant, reached Germany as a beta in October 2024 [s19][s20], answering product questions in German inside the app [s37]. In November 2026 German press reported that Rufus has been merged into **"Alexa for Shopping"** in the Amazon app and on Amazon.de [s21]. The assistant reads your title, bullets, A+ content, images, reviews and Q&A to answer questions like "Welche Trinkflasche ist spülmaschinenfest?" ("Which bottle is dishwasher-safe?"). Listings that clearly state facts in good German get recommended; vague listings get skipped.

blocks.h3: What this means for a beginner

ul: Germany is big, mature and competitive. You win with a **branded product that solves a specific problem**, not with the cheapest copy.
Fees in Europe fell slightly in 2026 [s2], but new surcharges (fuel, peak season) came in [s8][s10]. Model your margin with today's rate card, not a 2024 YouTube video.
Germany is also your base for the rest of the EU. One Amazon Europe account lets you list in other EU stores later (see "grow").
Compliance (VAT, packaging registration, product safety) is stricter than in the US. Budget time for it before your first shipment.

callout.title: No inbound placement fee in Europe (yet)
callout.text: Unlike the US, the European rate card has no inbound placement fee and no excess inventory fee. Amazon controls how much you send with capacity limits instead [s4].

sections.title: Is Amazon Germany right for you?

ul: You want to sell in the EU. Germany is the largest Amazon store in Europe [s14] and the usual hub for Pan-European FBA [s7].
You have (or will build) a brand and can get German-language packaging, labels and listings right.
You can handle VAT registration and monthly filings, or will pay an accountant to do it.
Your product is light and standard-size. German FBA fees for parcels under 900 g start around €3.39–€3.44 [s4], which works for items selling at €20 or more.
Your product is very cheap and generic: Haul and Temu set the price expectations [s22].
Your product is electrical, has batteries, is a toy, a cosmetic or food. All are possible, but the paperwork is heavier (see "compliance").
You can't spend a few weeks on registrations before the first sale.

blocks.p: You do not need to live in Germany. Amazon's European account is open to sellers from many countries. What changes is tax and paperwork:

ul: **EU-based sellers** (e.g. from Poland, Netherlands, Austria) can use the EU's One-Stop-Shop (OSS) to declare VAT on cross-border sales to consumers in other EU countries through their home tax office [s28][s29]. But stock stored in a German warehouse means German VAT registration (see "tax").

**Non-EU sellers** (e.g. India, China, UK, US, Turkey) need a German VAT registration as soon as stock sits in German warehouses. German tax law gives non-EU businesses a centrally assigned tax office based on their home country [s34]. For some sales the marketplace itself becomes the "deemed supplier" and handles VAT (see "tax") [s30].

**From China and India** in particular: plan to ship inventory to Amazon in bulk (sea or air freight, cleared through EU customs) rather than sending single parcels. From July 2026 low-value parcels pay a flat €3 duty per item [s24], and an EU handling fee is coming [s26].
**From the UK**: Remote Fulfilment lets you sell UK-stored FBA stock to German, French, Italian and Spanish customers, for products priced up to €135 [s9].

blocks.p: Amazon.de pays out in euros. You need a bank account that can receive EUR payouts (a euro account in your country, a European account, or a payment service that gives you local EU bank details). You also need a credit or debit card that can be charged internationally for fees. Check which deposit methods Seller Central accepts for your country during registration.

blocks.h3: Common reasons for delays or rejection

ul: Names or addresses that differ between ID, bank statement and form (even a missing middle name).
Blurry scans, cropped corners, or documents that are expired or too old.
Using a virtual office or forwarding address as your main business address.
Opening a second account, or using a device, card or bank account linked to another seller account. Amazon treats related accounts strictly.
Using someone else's documents (a "rented" account). This leads to permanent bans.

callout.title: Pre-flight checklist
callout.text: Same name and address on ID, bank statement and card; documents in colour, all four corners visible; one computer and network you will keep using; a euro-capable bank account; time blocked for the verification call.

ul: **Low-inventory cost coverage fee (Pan-EU):** charged on standard-size products in Pan-European FBA when your stock falls below 28 days of supply across Germany, France, Italy and Spain [s6][s4]. Running out is expensive twice: lost sales plus this fee.

**Returns processing fee:** since February 2025 FBA returns in Europe can carry a processing fee, mainly for products with high return rates [s12]. In Germany shoppers return a lot, especially clothing, so this matters.

blocks.p: Cost per click (CPC, what you pay each time a shopper clicks your ad) varies widely by keyword and category. We did not find a reliable, current public average for Amazon.de, so look at the suggested bids in the Amazon Ads console for your own keywords before you set a budget.

sections.title: Tax and legal: VAT, OSS, customs and income tax

callout.title: Not tax advice
callout.text: VAT in the EU is the most common reason new sellers lose money or get blocked. Read this to understand the moving parts, then confirm your setup with a tax adviser (Steuerberater) who works with marketplace sellers.

blocks.p: VAT (value added tax; in German "Umsatzsteuer" or "Mehrwertsteuer") is charged on almost every sale to German consumers and is included in the price shoppers see. You collect it and pay it to the tax office, minus VAT you paid on business costs. Check the current German standard and reduced rates for your product category with your adviser; food, books and some other goods use the reduced rate.

blocks.h3: When do you need a German VAT registration?

ul: **You store stock in Germany** (FBA in German warehouses, including Pan-EU): you need a German VAT registration, because sales are made from German stock [s35].
**Pan-European FBA**: Amazon may store your stock in several countries, so you need VAT registrations in each storage country, typically Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Poland and Czechia [s35].
**EFN (European Fulfilment Network)**: stock stays in one country, so usually one registration, but higher fees on cross-border orders [s35][s7].

**Distance sales from another EU country**: there is a single EU-wide threshold of **€10,000** per year of cross-border sales to consumers. Below it you can charge your home-country VAT; above it you charge the customer's country VAT, usually declared through the **One-Stop-Shop (OSS)** [s28][s29]. The €10,000 limit replaced older national thresholds on 1 July 2021 [s28].

blocks.h3: Two German numbers: Steuernummer and USt-IdNr

blocks.p: When the German tax office registers you, you get a **Steuernummer** (tax number, used on your VAT returns). Marketplace sellers also need a **USt-IdNr** (VAT identification number, starting "DE"), which Amazon asks for. Since July 2021 marketplaces ask for a valid German VAT ID rather than the old paper certificate [s32].

From 2019, German law (§22f of the VAT Act) made marketplaces like Amazon collect a tax-office certificate from sellers, or risk being liable for unpaid VAT [s33]. Since July 2021 the valid German VAT ID replaced the certificate in practice [s32]. If an old guide tells you to request an "F22 certificate", it is out of date, but the principle remains: Amazon can block your German listings if your VAT details are missing or invalid.

blocks.h3: Non-EU sellers and the "deemed supplier" rule

blocks.p: Since July 2021, for certain sales by non-EU sellers, the marketplace is treated as the seller for VAT (the "deemed supplier"). The non-EU seller makes a zero-rated sale to the marketplace, and the marketplace makes the taxable sale to the consumer and pays the VAT [s30][s28]. This covers imported consignments of €150 or less, and B2C sales inside the EU by non-EU sellers from EU stock [s28][s30]. Even then, if your stock sits in a German warehouse you will usually still need a German VAT registration for imports and stock movements. Don't assume "Amazon handles VAT" means "I need no registration".
Non-EU businesses are handled by centrally assigned German tax offices based on their home country [s34]. Your adviser or the German tax administration can tell you which office covers your country.

Goods bought from outside the EU in consignments of up to €150 used to be free of customs duty. That exemption ended on 1 July 2026. A temporary flat **€3 duty per item** now applies to these low-value parcels until the EU customs data hub takes over [s24][s27], expected in 2028 [s27][s25]. A separate **€2 per item EU handling fee** applies from 1 November 2026, according to UK government guidance [s26]. For FBA sellers shipping in bulk, these rules mostly don't apply, because bulk imports already pay normal duty and import VAT. They matter if you ship single parcels from China or India straight to EU customers.

German-resident sole traders can use the small-business rule (Kleinunternehmerregelung) if turnover stayed under **€25,000 last year and stays under €100,000 this year**, the limits since 1 January 2025 [s31]. Once you cross €100,000 in the year, normal VAT applies from that sale on [s31]. Most Amazon FBA sellers outgrow this fast, and it doesn't help with VAT in other EU countries without extra steps.

ul: **German residents:** register a business (Gewerbeanmeldung) at your local town hall before you start; you then pay income tax, possibly trade tax, and VAT.

**Non-residents:** you normally pay income tax in your home country on profits. Germany taxes your VAT, not your income, unless you have a permanent establishment there. Ask your home-country accountant.
**Keep records:** Amazon's VAT transaction reports and settlement reports are what your accountant needs.

blocks.p: Before you send stock to Germany. A marketplace-experienced adviser will register your VAT number(s), file monthly or quarterly returns, handle OSS, and keep you out of trouble with Amazon's VAT checks.

sections.title: Product compliance: GPSR, CE, packaging, electronics, batteries, trademarks

blocks.p: The EU and Germany have more product rules than most marketplaces. Amazon checks many of them automatically and blocks listings that miss them. Do this work before you order stock, because labels and packaging must be right at the factory.

Some categories need Amazon's approval or extra documents before you can list: for example food and supplements, cosmetics, toys in peak season, medical devices and some electronics. Search your product in Seller Central ("Add a product") to see if approval is needed.

blocks.h3: GPSR and the EU Responsible Person

blocks.p: The EU **General Product Safety Regulation (GPSR)** applies to consumer products sold to EU customers, online and offline. In practice for Amazon sellers:

ul: Every product needs an **economic operator based in the EU** (a manufacturer, importer, authorised representative or fulfilment service provider) who is responsible for safety. If you are outside the EU, you appoint a service provider to act as your **EU Responsible Person**.

Your listing must show the manufacturer's name and contact details, the EU responsible person's details, product identifiers (type, batch or serial number), and warnings and safety information in German.
You enter this in Seller Central under "Manage Your Compliance". Missing GPSR data is a common reason listings are hidden.
Keep a product risk assessment and technical documentation, and act fast on safety complaints.

blocks.p: Many product types (toys, electrical and electronic goods, machinery, personal protective equipment, some cosmetics packaging rules aside) must carry the **CE mark**. It means the manufacturer declares the product meets the relevant EU directives. You need the EU Declaration of Conformity and test reports from an accredited lab. A CE mark without real testing is illegal and is one of the fastest ways to lose a listing after a customer complaint.
EPR (extended producer responsibility) means whoever first puts packaging or products on the German market pays for their recycling. Amazon.de asks for proof for the relevant categories.

ul: **Packaging (Verpackungsgesetz):** if you sell packaged goods to German consumers, register in the public **LUCID** register (run by the Zentrale Stelle Verpackungsregister) and sign a contract with a packaging compliance scheme ("duales System"). Enter your LUCID number in Seller Central. This applies to nearly every seller, including FBA sellers from abroad.

**Electrical and electronic equipment (ElektroG / WEEE):** register with **stiftung ear** before selling anything with a plug or battery-powered electronics, and print the crossed-out wheelie-bin symbol on the product. Non-German sellers need an authorised representative in Germany for this registration.

**Batteries:** products with batteries (including built-in ones) need battery registration with stiftung ear under German battery law, which is being updated to implement the EU Battery Regulation. Check the current rules before you list.

blocks.p: Your listing, safety warnings, instructions for use and labels should be in **German**. Use a native speaker or a professional translator, not raw machine translation: Alexa for Shopping and German customers both notice bad German [s21]. Units must be metric. Textile products need fibre content labelling. Cosmetics, food and toys have their own labelling rules.

German law requires businesses that sell online to show clear provider information (the "Impressum"): legal name, address, how to contact you quickly (email and usually phone), commercial register and VAT ID where applicable. On Amazon, this appears through your seller profile's business information, so fill in Seller Central's "Legal Information" section completely and keep it current. German competitors and associations can send costly warning letters ("Abmahnungen") for missing or wrong information.

ul: **Which trademark:** an **EU trademark (EUIPO)** covers all EU countries in one application; a **German trademark (DPMA)** covers Germany only and is usually cheaper. Both are accepted for Amazon Brand Registry.
**Timing:** registration takes months, partly because of an opposition period. Apply as early as possible, ideally before you order packaging with your brand name.

**Brand Registry** gives you A+ content, Brand Stores, Sponsored Brands ads, Brand Analytics, Vine and stronger protection against hijackers. You can enrol with a pending application in many cases; check the current rules in Brand Registry.

**IP Accelerator:** where available, Amazon's IP Accelerator connects you to vetted IP law firms and can give you Brand Registry benefits while your application is pending. Check if it covers EUIPO/DPMA filings for you.

callout.title: We could not verify fees and dates here
callout.text: Registration fees, processing times and the exact GPSR, battery and packaging rules change. Check EUIPO, DPMA, LUCID, stiftung ear and Amazon's Manage Your Compliance page for current details before you pay anyone.

sections.title: Choosing your first product with data

ul: **Price €20–€50.** Enough room to pay the referral fee, FBA fee and ads. Under €20, fees and Haul-level price expectations squeeze you [s22].
**Small and light.** Fits a standard parcel under 900 g, so the FBA fee is about €3.44 [s4].
**Not electrical, no batteries, not a toy, food or cosmetic** for your first product. Less certification and EPR work.
**Clear improvement possible.** Read 1–3 star reviews of top sellers to find what buyers hate. Fix it.
**Steady demand all year,** not just Christmas.
**Low return risk.** No sizing, no fragile glass.

blocks.p: Aim for at least **30% of the net price (after VAT) left after product cost, freight, Amazon fees and ads**. Many sellers use the "one-third rule": roughly a third for product and freight, a third for Amazon fees and ads, a third for profit.

ul: **Product Opportunity Explorer** (Seller Central): search volume, number of sellers, click share and price trends for a niche on Amazon.de.
**Brand Analytics** (after Brand Registry): Search Query Performance and top search terms in Germany.

Seasonal (Christmas only, summer only) or a fad.
Fragile, liquid, heavy or oversize: higher FBA fees and damage returns.
Gated categories or dangerous goods (aerosols, batteries, flammables).
Patented designs or famous brands' look-alikes: IP complaints can kill a listing overnight.
Needs lots of size variants (clothing) for a first product: high returns [s12].

Decide with your tax adviser.

Don't exceed about 3 months of stock outside Q4. Storage jumps to €52.20 per cubic metre in October–December [s1], and aged stock is surcharged from 241 days [s5].
Plan Q4 inventory to arrive by early October; warehouses get congested in peak season.
Lead time = production + freight + customs + Amazon check-in. From Asia by sea, plan for many weeks.

sections.title: The first 90 days, week by week

ul: Write the listing in German: title (brand + product + key feature + size/quantity), five bullet points answering the questions buyers ask, and backend search terms with synonyms and common misspellings.
Main image on a pure white background; 6–8 more images showing size, use, details and a comparison. Add a short video if you can.
Complete every attribute field (material, dimensions, care). Alexa for Shopping reads structured data [s21].
Fill GPSR and compliance info, LUCID number and any certificates.
If you have Brand Registry: build A+ content and a simple Brand Store.
Price slightly below your target for the launch period to win first sales, but never below cost.
Turn on Sponsored Products: one automatic campaign and one manual exact-match campaign (see "ads").
Enrol in **Amazon Vine** (Brand Registry needed): Amazon gives free units to trusted reviewers who post honest reviews. This is the only safe way to speed up first reviews.
Consider a coupon (a green "Spare X %" badge) to lift click-through.
Each week: download the search term report, add converting search terms to manual campaigns, add wasteful ones as negatives.
Answer customer questions and check returns reasons. Fix the listing if buyers misunderstand something.
Use "Request a Review" on every eligible order (or automate the same official request).
Move price toward your target as reviews come in.
Reorder stock based on actual sales velocity, keeping 28+ days of supply [s6].
Test a new main image or title against the old one ("Manage Your Experiments" with Brand Registry).

head: Checkpoint
What "good" looks like for a first product
rows: Listing indexed for main German keywords, first sales daily, first Vine reviews arriving, no compliance blocks
10+ reviews, rating 4.2+, ad spend steady, organic sales growing, return rate under control
Most sales organic, total ad spend a modest share of revenue, reorder placed, first profit month or clear path to it
table.note: These are rules of thumb, not Amazon benchmarks. Every category is different.

ul: **Sponsored Products:** ads for single products in search results and on product pages. Start here.
**Sponsored Brands:** a banner with your logo and several products at the top of search (needs Brand Registry).
**Sponsored Display:** retargeting and audience ads on and off Amazon (later).
**ACoS (advertising cost of sale)** = ad spend ÷ ad sales. Spend €30 to make €100 in ad sales = 30% ACoS.
**TACoS (total ACoS)** = ad spend ÷ total sales (ads + organic). It shows if ads are building organic sales. Falling TACoS over time is the goal.
Your **break-even ACoS** is your margin before ads. In the worked example in "product", that's very low, which tells you to fix price or cost before spending heavily.

ol: **Auto campaign**, low-to-moderate bid, to discover search terms.
**Manual exact campaign** with 5–15 main German keywords from Product Opportunity Explorer and the auto campaign.
**Manual phrase or broad campaign** with a few wider terms, lower bids.
**Product targeting** campaign aimed at competitor products where yours is clearly better or cheaper.

blocks.p: Start with a daily budget you can afford for 60 days without panic, for example €10–€20 a day across all campaigns. Use the Amazon Ads console's suggested bids as your starting point and adjust weekly.

Negative keywords stop your ad showing for searches that waste money. Add irrelevant terms (wrong product type, other brands you don't compete with, "gebraucht" (used), "kostenlos" (free)), and search terms with many clicks and no sales.
During launch, an ACoS above your break-even is normal because you're buying data and rank. After about 60 days, aim to bring ACoS near your break-even on main keywords and cut what doesn't convert.

ol: Download the search term report for the last 7–14 days.
Move converting search terms into exact campaigns.
Add non-converting, high-click terms as negatives.
Lower bids on keywords far above target ACoS, raise slightly on profitable ones.
Check budget: campaigns running out of money by midday on profitable terms need more.
Check TACoS trend and stock level: never advertise a product about to go out of stock.

ul: **Amazon Vine** for early reviews (Brand Registry).
**Request a Review** button in Seller Central, or an inserted card that asks neutrally for honest feedback (never for a positive review, never with an incentive).
Fix the product and listing based on what reviews say. That raises the rating more than anything else.

blocks.p: A Brand Store gives you a free mini-site on Amazon.de to send traffic to. Brand Analytics shows what Germans search for in your category. Both need Brand Registry.

blocks.p: With one European Seller Central account you can list in other EU stores. The usual order: Austria buys from Amazon.de directly; then France, Italy and Spain (big, Pan-EU core markets [s6]); then the Netherlands, Poland, Sweden, Belgium and Ireland, smaller stores where competition can be lower. Ireland had promotional FBA rates with a 50% discount on local and Pan-EU fees in 2026 [s8].

ul: **Translate properly:** each store needs listings in its own language (Dutch for NL, Polish for PL, Swedish for SE, French or Dutch for BE, English for IE).
**Start with EFN** to test demand from your German stock with one VAT registration [s35][s7].
**Move to Pan-European FBA** when a country sells well: local fees and faster delivery, but VAT registrations where stock is stored [s7][s35].
**Compliance travels with you:** GPSR covers the whole EU, but packaging EPR is country by country (France, Spain and others have their own schemes).
**Remote Fulfilment** connects UK and EU stores for products up to €135 [s9].

sections.title: The most common beginner mistakes (and how to avoid them)

ol: **Sending stock to Germany without a German VAT number.** Amazon can block your listings and the tax office can claim back VAT. Register first [s35][s32].
**No LUCID packaging registration.** Required for nearly every seller of packaged goods to German consumers; Amazon checks it.
**Missing GPSR information** (manufacturer, EU responsible person, German safety info). Listings get suppressed.
**Fake or missing CE paperwork.** A complaint or market-surveillance check removes the product and can cost you the stock.
**Bad German.** Machine-translated listings lose sales and confuse Alexa for Shopping [s21].
**Ignoring fee changes.** Using old FBA rates instead of the 2026 card plus fuel and peak surcharges [s4][s8].
**Over-stocking before Q4.** Storage nearly doubles from October [s1][s11], and aged stock is surcharged from 241 days [s5].
**Running out of stock.** You lose ranking and, in Pan-EU, pay the low-inventory fee below 28 days of supply [s6].

**Review manipulation.** Paying for reviews, "free product for 5 stars", review groups, or asking friends and family. Amazon suspends accounts for this and German consumer law also forbids fake reviews. Use Vine and Request a Review only.
**Opening a second account or using a "rented" one.** Related or borrowed accounts get suspended.
**Copying a famous design or brand.** IP complaints remove listings fast; repeated complaints suspend accounts.
**Inauthentic or condition complaints.** Keep invoices from your supplier; Amazon may ask for them to prove authenticity.
**Late shipments and cancellations on FBM.** Keep late shipment rate and cancellation rate within Amazon's account health targets, or use FBA.
**Missing Impressum/business information.** Fill in Seller Central's legal information completely to avoid German warning letters.
**Shipping small parcels from Asia directly to EU customers.** Since July 2026 each low-value item pays €3 duty [s24], plus a €2 handling fee from November 2026 [s26].

faq.q: Can I sell on Amazon.de if I don't live in Germany?
faq.a: Yes. Sellers from India, China, the UK, the US and many other countries sell on Amazon.de. You need a European seller account, a euro-capable bank account, and usually a German VAT number once your stock sits in German warehouses. Non-EU sellers also need an EU Responsible Person for product safety.

faq.q: How much does it cost to start selling on Amazon Germany?
faq.a: The Professional plan is €39 a month plus VAT, or €0.99 per item on the Individual plan. On top come referral fees (mostly about 8–15%), FBA fees from about €2.33 for a light envelope to €3.44 for a standard parcel under 900 g, storage, ads and stock. A realistic first product launch often needs €4,000–€6,000 including inventory, registrations and ads.

faq.q: Do I need a German VAT number to sell on Amazon.de?
faq.a: If you use FBA and Amazon stores your goods in Germany, yes. If you ship from another EU country and stay under the €10,000 EU-wide distance-selling threshold, you may not need one. Amazon checks VAT details and can block listings without them.

faq.q: Does Amazon pay the VAT for me?
faq.a: Only in some cases. For certain sales by non-EU sellers, Amazon is the 'deemed supplier' and collects and pays the VAT. But you usually still need a VAT registration for stock stored in Germany, imports and returns. Ask a tax adviser before you send stock.

faq.q: What is LUCID and do I really need it?
faq.a: LUCID is Germany's public packaging register. If you sell packaged goods to German consumers, you must register and pay a packaging scheme for recycling. Amazon asks for your LUCID number, and selling without it can get your listings blocked.

faq.q: What is GPSR and what do I need for Amazon?
faq.a: GPSR is the EU's General Product Safety Regulation. Your listings must show the manufacturer, an EU-based responsible person, product identifiers and safety information in the local language. Enter it in Seller Central under Manage Your Compliance.

faq.q: Is Pan-European FBA worth it for a beginner?
faq.a: Usually not on day one. Pan-EU gives local fees across the EU but requires VAT registrations in every country where stock is stored (often six). Start with Germany, test other countries with EFN, and switch to Pan-EU once you have steady sales.

faq.q: Do I need to write my listings in German?
faq.a: Yes. German shoppers expect German, and safety information must be in German. Amazon's AI shopping assistant also reads your listing to answer questions, so clear, natural German helps you get recommended.

faq.q: Do I need a trademark to sell on Amazon.de?
faq.a: Not to sell, but you need one for Brand Registry, which unlocks A+ content, Vine, Brand Stores, Sponsored Brands and brand protection. An EU trademark covers all EU countries; a German DPMA trademark covers only Germany. Apply early because it takes months.

faq.q: What happened to the €150 customs exemption?
faq.a: It ended on 1 July 2026. Low-value parcels from outside the EU now pay a flat €3 duty per item, and an extra €2 handling fee applies from November 2026. Bulk FBA imports already paid normal duty, so this mostly hurts direct parcel shipping.

faq.q: What are the peak season fees on Amazon.de?
faq.a: From 15 October 2026 to 14 January 2027, Amazon adds a peak fee of about €0.21–€0.44 per unit on small and standard parcels in Germany. Storage also rises to €52.20 per cubic metre per month from October to December. Build both into your Q4 prices.

faq.q: How long does Amazon.de account verification take?
faq.a: It varies from a few days to several weeks. Delays usually come from mismatched names or addresses, blurry documents or missing the video verification call. Prepare matching documents and book the earliest call slot.

faq.q: Can I sell in Austria with my Amazon.de account?
faq.a: Austrian shoppers commonly buy from Amazon.de, so your German listings reach them. VAT rules still apply for sales to Austrian consumers, so check with your tax adviser how the EU distance-selling and OSS rules apply to you.

faq.q: Will Amazon Haul compete with my products?
faq.a: Haul sells ultra-cheap items up to €20, bought and imported by Amazon itself, not by third-party sellers. It doesn't take your listings, but it lowers price expectations for generic products. Choose a branded product that solves a real problem.
